newsitem.title: RUSSIA: BASKETBALL-MONEY TROUBLES MAR CSKA'S RUSSIAN TITLE.
newsitem.headline: BASKETBALL-MONEY TROUBLES MAR CSKA'S RUSSIAN TITLE.

text.p: When CSKA took their sixth consecutive Russian title at the weekend, booking their place in next season's potentially lucrative EuroLeague, the Moscow club's professionals were doing it for love, not money.

The players, who secured the championship in the fifth and final game of the play-offs against Avtodor Saratov on Sunday, have not been paid for nearly six months, underscoring the severe cash crisis facing Russian basketball.
"If the situation doesn't change within a month, I'm afraid we could lose this team," CSKA head coach Stanislav Yeryomin said. Top players are already looking at foreign contracts.

The Soviet Union, though always in the shadow of the Americans, were a major force in world basketball, winning Olympic golds in 1972 and 1988. But since the break-up of the country and the independence of the Baltic states, which bred many top Soviet players, the Russian game has faded.
Despite claiming their sixth league crown since 1992 with their win over Avtodor Saratov, CSKA face an uncertain future.

Players and coaching staff have not received a monthly pay packet from the club, which is owned by the Russian armed forces, since December. The prospects are not good for a quick improvement and some top players are looking for teams abroad.
"Our congratulations from the management included a few pennies bonus for the victory and a pat on the back," said CSKA starting point guard Sergei Bazarevich.
"We also got a promise to get our money back within a month but that sounds more like a broken record now."
"It's no secret some of our top players like Bazarevich and (Igor) Kudelin are looking elsewhere, hoping to sign a lucrative deal abroad," head coach Yeryomin said.
"If we don't find real money to honour players' contracts sometime soon, others will follow them."
The coach said he too had considered a move to one of leading European teams: "I could easily make two or three times more money in places like Greece or Turkey."
Earlier this season, CSKA'S city rivals Dynamo Moscow had a similar money crisis and Spartak St Petersburg seemed on the verge of going bankrupt before being rescued.
Money troubles have not helped international performances.
After a Final Four appearance in the European Champions' Cup last year in Paris, CSKA failed to make it into the second round of this season's inaugural EuroLeague competition.
Dynamo's poor showing this season meant Russian clubs will lose one of their two spots among the Europe's elite. CSKA will be Russia's sole representative in the EuroLeague next season.

One brighter note for the Russian game, however, sounded this week from an unlikely source. Moscow rolled out the red carpet for former NBA great Karim Abdul-Jabbar, who is holding a one-week basketball camp for promising Russian youngsters.
